summary: Defines a data structure that can be appended to selected ICMP messages to identify the interface a datagram arrived on, the interface it would have been forwarded through, and the next hop. This helps with troubleshooting. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router sends an error note, it adds which door the packet came through and where it would have gone next.

questions: how to identify next hop in icmp
what is icmp interface information object
how does traceroute identify the incoming interface
what is class-num 2 in icmp extensions
subtitle: A way for routers to say, inside an ICMP error, which interface a packet came in on and where it would have gone next.

tldr.problem: An ICMP error message often does not reveal which interface the failed datagram arrived on, especially for unnumbered interfaces, so traceroute and similar tools cannot name the exact interface.
tldr.mechanism: An Interface Information Object (Class-Num 2) is appended to selected ICMP messages. Its C-Type bits say whether it describes the incoming interface, a sub-IP component, the outgoing interface or the next hop, and which of ifIndex, IP address, name and MTU follow.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools get explicit interface and next-hop details for troubleshooting. The RFC says the extension is meant for administrative debugging, and implementations should be able to suppress or hide the information.

today: RFC 5837 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2010. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this entry.

sections.title: Why ICMP Needs Interface Information
sections.content:
IP devices use ICMP (ICMPv4 in RFC 792, ICMPv6 in RFC 4443) to report problems. In the simplest case, the source address of an ICMP message identifies the interface the datagram arrived on. In many cases it does not.

For ICMPv4, RFC 1812 requires the source address to be one of the addresses of the interface the message is sent over. That only names the incoming interface if the message leaves through the same interface and that interface is numbered. Incoming and outgoing interfaces can differ because of asymmetric link costs, parallel links or Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP). When the datagram arrives on an unnumbered interface, neither ICMPv4 nor ICMPv6 can identify it, and the receiver cannot tell whether the source address happens to match.

The extension in this RFC identifies interfaces explicitly. It builds on the ICMP multi-part message framework of RFC 4884, so the same backward compatibility issues apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the return address on an error note does not say which door the packet used. Sometimes the door has no name at all, so this adds a clear label.

sections.title: What Can Be Identified and Why
sections.content:
An interface can be identified by any combination of ifIndex, IPv4 address, IPv6 address, name and MTU. The ifIndex is the 32-bit value from the Interfaces Group MIB (RFC 2863). The name SHOULD be the first 63 octets of the ifName.

The same extension can describe the outgoing interface the datagram would have used if it had been deliverable, and the next-hop IP address it would have been sent to. Next-hop information may not always be available, so the RFC only defines the encoding for when it is.

The main use is an enhanced traceroute, which can show at each node the incoming interface, a sub-IP component of it, the outgoing interface and the next hop. The ifIndex can also serve as an opaque token to tell whether two ICMP messages from one router involve the same interface. A second use is policy and MTU diagnosis: for example, learning which outgoing interface an access control list acted on, or which interface cannot support a given MTU in Path MTU Discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: A traceroute can now say not just which router a packet visited but exactly which door it used. That helps people find which door is broken or too narrow.

sections.title: The Interface Information Object
sections.content:
The Interface Information Object is an ICMP extension object with a Class-Num of 2. It may be appended to ICMPv4 Time Exceeded, Destination Unreachable and Parameter Problem messages, and to ICMPv6 Time Exceeded and Destination Unreachable messages. It cannot be appended to other ICMP messages, for reasons given in RFC 4884.

The object MAY be appended to those messages, and SHOULD be appended whenever needed to identify an unnumbered interface, unless local policy or security considerations say otherwise. One message can carry from zero to four instances, one for each interface role.

The data inside an object does not label itself, so the order is fixed. If present, the pieces come in this order: the 32-bit ifIndex, the IP Address Sub-Object, the Interface Name Sub-Object, and the 32-bit MTU. Any data after them MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small form with four optional boxes: door number, address, name and size limit. The boxes must always be filled in the same order.

sections.title: The C-Type Bits and Sub-Objects
sections.content:
The C-Type byte of the object says both the role and what data is present. Bits 0-1 are the Interface Role: 0 is the incoming IP interface, 1 is a sub-IP component of the incoming interface (such as a link aggregation group member), 2 is the outgoing interface and 3 is the IP next hop. Bits 2 and 3 are reserved, MUST be 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt. Bit 4 means ifIndex is included, bit 5 an IP Address Sub-Object, bit 6 a Name Sub-Object and bit 7 an MTU.

The IP Address Sub-Object has a 16-bit Address Family Identifier (1 for a 32-bit IPv4 address, 2 for a 128-bit IPv6 address), a 16-bit Reserved field set to zero, and then the address. An IPv4 eliciting datagram requires an IPv4 address, and an IPv6 one an IPv6 address.

The Interface Name Sub-Object starts with a length octet that counts itself and the name. The length MUST be a multiple of 4 octets and MUST NOT exceed 64. The name is UTF-8 and is padded with ASCII NULL characters to a 4-octet boundary.

Receiving an object with bits 4 to 7 all 0 is valid and MUST NOT cause a warning or error.
sections.plainLanguage: One row of eight switches says which door this describes and which boxes are filled in. The address box says if it is the old or new kind of address, and the name box says how long the name is.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows a full ICMPv4 Time Exceeded message with an Interface Information Object after the original datagram, preceded by the extension structure header and object header from RFC 4884. Its examples use the maximum name length of 64 octets for illustration only.

  • Incoming interface by ifIndex and name: C-Type 00001010b, length 72 (4 + 4 + 64).
  • Incoming interface by ifIndex, IPv4 address and name: C-Type 00001110b, length 80 (4 + 4 + 8 + 64).
  • Incoming interface by ifIndex and IPv6 address: C-Type 00001100b, length 28 (4 + 4 + 20).
  • Outgoing interface by ifIndex and name: C-Type 10001010b, length 72 (4 + 4 + 64).
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show filled-in forms. Each one has a code that says which door it is about and which boxes were used.

sections.title: Usage Rules and NAT
sections.content:
Several objects can be in one message only if each has a unique role. ifIndex, MTU and name MAY be included when available, but no more than one of each per object. One IP address may be included only when it matches the family of the eliciting datagram and the interface has such an address. A message with two objects of the same role, or with a duplicate element in one role, is illegal and MUST be silently discarded.

The RFC also covers Network Address Translation. NAT devices MUST NOT translate or overwrite these extensions; they MUST either remove the extension or pass it unchanged. Because addresses inside the extension may then be of a different realm than those in the datagram header, applications should not assume they are the same. A NAT that translates between ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 could also leave an IPv4 address in an ICMPv6 message, or the reverse.
sections.plainLanguage: You may not put two labels for the same door on one note, and a note that does is thrown away. Address-changing boxes on the way must not edit these labels.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Controls
sections.content:
The extension gives traceroute users network information that was not available before. Implementations SHOULD offer configuration switches that suppress the extension by role (incoming interface, outgoing interface, sub-IP data) and switches that hide kinds of information such as ifIndex or interface name.

An implementation could choose what to include based on the destination of the ICMP message: for example, the IP address for everyone, but ifIndex and name only for a management address of the network. Detailed information might go to destinations in the local administrative domain and only traditional information to external or untrusted ones.

The intended use is administrative debugging and troubleshooting, not other applications. The RFC specifies no authentication mechanism, and warns that ICMP messages and their contents are easily spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can choose who gets the extra labels, so strangers only see the plain note. And anyone can fake a note, so do not trust it blindly.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has reserved Class-Num 2 for the Interface Information Object in the ICMP Extension Object Classes registry. From its C-Type, IANA reserved bits 0-1 for the Interface Role, bits 2 and 3 as unallocated (allocatable with Standards Action), and bits 4 to 7 for ifIndex, IP Address Sub-Object, Name Sub-Object and MTU.

The Interface Role values are 0 for Incoming IP Interface, 1 for Sub-IP Component of Incoming IP Interface, 2 for Outgoing IP Interface and 3 for IP Next Hop.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers now has an entry for this form, with each switch and door number written down.

items.desc: The IP interface on which the datagram arrived.

items.desc: For example a link aggregation group member.

items.label: Outgoing IP interface

items.label: IP next hop
items.desc: The next hop the datagram would have been forwarded to.

items.desc: An IP Address Sub-Object is present.

items.desc: An Interface Name Sub-Object is present.
